slides.title: What "distant reading" has meant
slides.lead: Moretti, Underwood, the Voyant tradition. What Claude Projects adds: persistent context across multi-turn conversation, multi-file uploads, native handling of mixed formats.

slides.title: Two genealogies, one method
bullets: **Moretti, 2000s:** the literary system at scale — what a single book hides, a thousand reveal.
**Underwood, 2010s–:** stylometrics, character networks, century-long trends.
**Voyant, classroom:** word counts and concordances democratized to the seminar room.
Claude Projects: multi-text, multi-format, multi-turn — humanities-scale, not big-data scale.

slides.title: Where AI is reading text right now
slides.lead: Three quick scenes from professional reading practices already on the move.

slides.title: Killing the billable hour
bullets: Eudia and other legal-tech startups pitching AI as the end of the billable hour.
Reuters: AI is now an LA law student.
When a profession decides 'reading' is automatable, what gets lost?

slides.title: Reading the doctor's notes
bullets: Rolling Stone: AI chatbot medical-advice study.
Patients reading test results with Claude before they call the office.
What does it mean for our students that *every* domain now uses an LLM intermediary?

slides.title: The cheating frame is the wrong frame
bullets: Futurism: students openly use ChatGPT for homework.
OpenAI tracks the use as growth, not failure.
Our problem isn't enforcement. Our problem is teaching reading as a *practice* students can do *with* the tool.

slides.title: Whose reading paid for this?
slides.lead: Distant reading at this scale was always built on hidden labor. With LLMs, the labor moved — but didn't vanish.

slides.quote: Time reported that OpenAI had subcontracted Kenyan workers making less than two dollars a day to filter out gore, hate speech, child sexual abuse material, and pornographic images from ChatGPT and OpenAI's image-generation tool.
slides.attribution: Bender & Hanna, on the labor that made the chatbot polite

slides.title: The training set is also a legal record
bullets: August 2025: authors celebrate a historic settlement in the Anthropic class action.
The training corpus is the legal exhibit.
Where does *your* writing sit inside that record?

slides.title: Live demo: Claude Projects
slides.lead: A small corpus I have not opened before. We walk: preprocessing → bag-of-words → key phrases → comparative passages → thematic network.

slides.title: A corpus I haven't opened
slides.note: Watch the iteration. Notice when I push back, ask Claude to reconsider, point out a mistake. The iteration is the humanities work.

slides.title: Distant reading with Claude Projects
slides.prompt: Using the three-to-five-text corpus you brought:
steps: Create a fresh Project. Upload all texts.
Run the sequence: stopword filter → bag-of-words → key phrases → character or theme network → comparative read.
Ask Claude for an **Artifact** that visualizes one finding (a frequency chart, a network, a comparative table).
Critique what you see. Compare to what close reading would surface.
**Document at least one place Claude got it wrong.** That's the deliverable.

slides.quote: The point of this exercise is not the visualization. The point is the iteration. Notice when you have to push back, refine, ask Claude to reconsider. That iteration is the actual humanities work — and it is teachable.

slides.title: End in an Artifact
bullets: Word cloud, frequency chart, network diagram, comparative table.
Artifacts are *small interactive web pages* — Claude can build one in a single turn.
They're shareable to a class, a colleague, a Twitter thread.
Save the URL — we revisit Artifacts in Workshop 3.

slides.title: Where Claude *will* fail
bullets: Confabulating quotes that aren't in the source.
Smoothing genre or period differences into a fake consensus.
Quietly losing files when the conversation grows.
**Your job in this exercise is to find one of these.**

slides.title: Scaffolding for students
bullets: Require *three prompts* documented before the result they used.
Require an annotated screenshot of one bad answer.
Require a one-paragraph reflection: *what did close reading catch that this missed?*
Grade the iteration, not the artifact.

slides.title: Discussion
slides.lead: Where did Claude help? Where did it hallucinate? What would a student need to know before they used this for an assignment in your course?

slides.title: Bring forward to Workshop 3
bullets: Save your Project. We'll add images to it next time.
Save the *bad* Claude answer you found — it's a teaching artifact.
Workshop 3 (Week 5): we move from text to image. Bring 5–10 images you have rights to use.

slides.title: Carry it forward
slides.lead: The Project you built today is yours. Add to it across the semester; it's the closest thing this workshop offers to a portable workspace.
